10 most haunted places in Hong Kong to visit—if you dare!

By Jianne Soriano and Fashila Kanakka
Published: Oct 23, 2026 10:25 AM HKT, 10 min read
Listen to audio version of this article
0:00 / 0:00 Instaread
Sponsored by

Hong Kong is home to magnificent skyscrapers and historical buildings. But amidst the bustling cityscape also lies terrifying locations with a spooky past. Sure, some of these spots may be tucked away in a village in The Territories, but you’ll be surprised to find that some are right in the heart of the city. But easily overlooked. From a decaying mansion to an abandoned school, these are the most haunted places in Hong Kong.

Beyond its food and shopping, the city has eerie spots that ghost hunters rank alongside famous haunts abroad, Tat Tak School and Bride’s Pool among them.

Most have a dark past, from a former mental hospital to wartime killings, and some are private property, so stay respectful and safe at Halloween, during the Hungry Ghost Festival or any time.

These are the most haunted places in Hong Kong

1 /10

Tat Tak School

Often called the city’s most haunted abandoned school, it began at the Yu Kiu ancestral hall, Ping Shan, in 1931, until British forces moved students out in 1961, and the site endured the Japanese occupation and massacres. It moved to its Yuen Long building in 1974 and closed in 1998.

Local legend links it to a death involving its principal, and visitors report sightings, including a student who became hysterical on one exploration.

(Photo credit: hkurbex/Facebook)

Additional Information

Address:
Tat Tak School, Ping Shan, Yuen Long, Hong Kong
2 /10

Dragon Lodge

This empty Peak mansion had several owners, one bankrupt and one who died there, before the Japanese military occupied it. Renovation workers told of ghostly encounters, and ghost hunters became so common that security was increased.

(Photo credit: hkurbex/Facebook)

Additional Information

Address:
Dragon Lodge, 32 Lugard Road, The Peak, Hong Kong
3 /10

Sai Ying Pun Community Complex

Known as the High Street Ghost House, it housed nurses after World War II and in 1974 became a psychiatric facility, the first and largest of its kind.

Overcrowding and stigma marked its hospital years; it was later abandoned and hit by two fires, though the granite facade remains. Wartime soldiers are also believed to have killed people there.

(Image credit: ystsoi/Flickr)

Additional Information

Address:
2 High Street, Sai Ying Pun, Hong Kong
4 /10

Nam Koo Terrace

Built in 1915 by a wealthy Shanghai family and now a Grade I historic building, it was used as a military brothel by Japanese forces in the war. Ghost stories grew after owner To Chak-man died there of unknown causes; a 1993 Hopewell Holdings hotel plan never went ahead.

(Photo credit: fong_manson /Flickr)

Additional Information

Address:
55 Ship Street, Wan Chai, Hong Kong
5 /10

Murray House

Built around the 1840s as British officers’ quarters in the Murray Barracks, it became a Japanese headquarters and prison from 1941, where up to 4,000 people are thought to have been executed.

After exorcisms in 1963 and 1974, it was dismantled in 1982 and rebuilt in Stanley, with fewer sightings since.

(Photo credit: snuffy /Flickr)

Additional Information

Address:
96 Stanley Main Street, Stanley, Hong Kong
6 /10

So Lo Pun

This remote Hakka village in the northeast stands abandoned, and no one has confirmed why its residents left.

Its name means “locked compass”, after reports that compasses fail there; theories range from illness to a massacre or a boat accident.

(Photo credit: Bergman /Flickr)

Additional Information

Address:
So Lo Pun, Plover Cove Country Park, Sha Tau Kok, Hong Kong
7 /10

Bride’s Pool

Legend says a bride travelling to her groom’s village drowned at the waterfall when a porter slipped, and that her spirit remains.

A 1982 murder, four nearby car accidents in 2008 and another death in 2016 added to its reputation.

(Photo credit: Davis Kwan /Flickr)

Additional Information

Address:
Bride’s Pool, Plover Cove Country Park, Shuen Wan, New Territories, Hong Kong
8 /10

Braid Road, CUHK

A well-known campus legend from the 1960s tells of a young girl fleeing Mainland China without a train ticket who died in a railway accident.

The road runs through CUHK between Shaw College and Chung Chi College, where people claim to have seen a weeping, faceless girl.

(Photo credit: @shali/Unsplash)

Additional Information

Address:
Braid Road, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Sha Tin, Hong Kong
9 /10

Bela Vista Villa

These Cheung Chau holiday homes are tied to a legend of a woman in traditional Chinese dress who died in one villa, followed by further deaths nearby.

About 26 sites were reportedly affected, a ghostly woman is said to appear near the beach, and deaths fell after a rename to “Miami Resort”.

(Photo credit: Booking.com)

Additional Information

Address:
Cheung Chau Beach Road (North), Cheung Chau, Hong Kong
10 /10

Cheung Sha Wan Abattoir

One of the city’s three main slaughterhouses, it closed in 1999 and was meant to become an arts compound, but artists said it was haunted. The arts hub moved to what is now Cattle Depot Artist Village in To Kwa Wan, leaving the abattoir to decay.

(Photo credit: hkurbex/Facebook)

Additional Information

Address:
757 Lai Chi Kok Road, Cheung Sha Wan, Hong Kong

(Featured image credit: @cyppoon/Flickr, Hero image credit: @123741708@N02/Flickr)
